title: Accelerating SREs to On-Call and Beyond
subtitle: Build on-call readiness through structured practice and trust
summary: Training an SRE means developing the ability to reason about unfamiliar failures, not merely learning a list of operating procedures. A cumulative learning path gives newcomers a clear route through the service and gives mentors evidence of progress. Reverse engineering, comparative diagnosis, and postmortem study build models that support improvisation. Disaster role-play and contained hands-on breakages let trainees practice before they carry full incident responsibility. Updating documentation with experts turns gaps into shared learning. Shadow shifts expose real decisions, while reverse shadowing lets a newcomer lead with experienced support. On-call readiness is an important milestone rather than the end of education; growing project ownership and continuing team learning keep both newcomers and experienced engineers effective as production changes.

concepts.title: An ordered learning path
concepts.body: A training plan should progress through service concepts and practical tasks in a sequence the learner can understand. It can follow the request path, naming relevant documents, expert contacts, and questions that demonstrate comprehension. Mentors assess understanding rather than merely completed reading. This gives newcomers visible progress and helps the team agree on what readiness for operational responsibility actually means.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A trainee traces a request from ingress through storage and explains which dependencies can fail without losing the main response.

concepts.title: Reasoning beyond procedures
concepts.body: Runbooks cannot anticipate every incident, so training should develop reverse engineering, comparison, and hypothesis testing. Learners inspect instrumentation, reconstruct component relationships, and explain what observations support their model. Comparing healthy and unhealthy cases narrows possibilities under pressure. Presenting findings to an expert also reveals outdated assumptions in the team’s existing understanding, making education useful to both parties.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A new engineer diagrams the live dependency graph and discovers a fallback path missing from the team’s architecture document.

concepts.title: Practice failures before primary responsibility
concepts.body: Postmortems expose past failure mechanisms; role-play lets a group explain investigation and mitigation choices; contained breakage develops familiarity with real tools. These methods complement one another. A realistic isolated stack can be impaired while learners predict and observe its response, creating experience without making their first genuine page the first time they have diagnosed a failing service.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A staging dependency is made unresponsive, and trainees compare predicted resource exhaustion with the metrics they actually see.

concepts.title: Shadowing, documentation, and continuing ownership
concepts.body: Shadow on-call shifts let trainees observe real incidents and discuss decisions afterward without owning the immediate response. Reverse shadowing gives the learner responsibility with an experienced engineer available to help. Pairing newcomers with experts to revise documentation spreads knowledge and builds trust. Project ownership should grow alongside operational skill, while ongoing technical sessions keep the whole team current after qualification.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A trainee leads a supported shift, then coauthors its postmortem and corrects the training material that missed a relevant failure mode.

misconceptions.claim: A ticket queue is a complete training curriculum.
misconceptions.correction: Random interrupts omit systematic understanding and can overwhelm capable learners before they develop a service model.

misconceptions.claim: Qualification for on-call finishes SRE training.
misconceptions.correction: Production evolves, so experienced engineers also need continuing education and opportunities to refresh their assumptions.

scenario.title: Train an engineer for real duty
scenario.context: A new SRE understands the service code but has never handled a page. Two senior engineers are available for one rotation and the service has a complicated recovery procedure.

options.label: Use shadowing, a bounded practice incident, then paired duty
options.benefit: Training converts implicit expertise into observed operational skill.
options.cost: Senior time is required and practice can expose simulated faults.
options.consequence: The learner handles a rehearsed failover with a mentor before taking solo duty.

options.label: Put the new engineer alone on the next rotation
options.benefit: The new engineer gains direct experience quickly.
options.cost: A real incident becomes the first rehearsal with customer impact.
options.consequence: The learner escalates late and the senior must reconstruct context.

scenario.debrief: Code familiarity alone does not establish incident readiness. Combine a service learning path, realistic practice, and observed shifts, then let the learner lead with support before relying on independent response.

quiz.question: What should an on-call learning checklist primarily establish?
options: An ordered set of knowledge and comprehension outcomes
A count of tickets closed regardless of subject
quiz.explanation: The plan develops transferable understanding and makes readiness assessable.

quiz.question: What is reverse shadowing?
options: A newcomer follows an experienced responder and compares notes afterward
A mentor leads a simulated incident while the trainee watches
The newcomer leads while an experienced engineer remains available to support
quiz.explanation: It provides a supported transition from observation to responsibility.

quiz.question: Why ask a newcomer to reconstruct a service diagram?
options: It develops discovery skills and can uncover stale expert assumptions
It removes the need for expert review
It proves every possible incident is understood
quiz.explanation: Independent reconstruction tests both the learner’s reasoning and the team’s existing model.

exercise.prompt: Design a short progression for an engineer who knows the code but has not operated the service.

steps.text: Trace the service and explain its critical dependencies.
Diagnose contained failures before carrying primary responsibility.
Observe real responses and compare reasoning with experienced operators.
Take responsibility with support, then continue learning and owning projects.
